The first thing Ada Vale learned about keeping a public clock was that nobody wanted to know the time. They wanted to know whether they were late. A man running uphill would call, “Is that right?” and point at the clock above the market. If Ada said yes, he ran faster. If she explained that the minute hand was accurate but the hour hand had slipped its collar, he went on running at much the same speed. Eventually she learned to call back, “You’ve got a minute.” This was generally true in one sense or another, and it seemed to help.

The clock had four faces. The north face overlooked the station, the east the wholesale flower market, the south a row of apartments, and the west a brick wall erected in 1974 by a bank that had neglected to look up. Every Thursday Ada climbed eighty-six steps with her lunch, a flask of tea, and whatever tools the maintenance book suggested. She ate behind the west face. Here the afternoon sun came reflected off the bank in a dim red square, like the light inside a closed eyelid. Of all the rooms she had known, including rooms in houses she had owned, this was the one where she felt least obliged to improve herself.

In March the council sent a woman named Lecia to inspect the tower. Lecia wore white trainers and carried no clipboard, which made Ada underestimate her. She climbed the stairs without stopping. At the top she put one palm against the winding drum and closed her eyes. “My father had a printing press,” she said. “Different noise. Same feeling in your teeth.” Then she measured everything, including the width of the trapdoor, and took a photograph of the place where Ada had pencilled the dates of every new pair of work boots on the wall. Ada had no explanation for having done this. Lecia did not ask for one.

The proposal arrived six weeks later. The market needed a new roof. To pay for some of it, the council would lease the tower to a communications company. The mechanism would be removed and the four hands driven by small electric motors. A receiver would keep them precisely synchronized. There would be no winding, no weekly visit, no possibility of the station face gaining three minutes whenever a hard frost came up the valley. Ada read the letter twice. Then she sat at her kitchen table and ate six dry crackers, one after another, though a tub of perfectly good butter stood within reach.

She was sixty-eight. She could afford to lose the money, although not, as her brother put it, to an extent that justified mentioning it quite so often. What she could not picture was Thursday. Monday she swam. On Tuesdays and Wednesdays she repaired domestic clocks in a little shop that smelled of wet coats even in July. Friday was groceries and her brother’s lunch. Thursday had a staircase in it. Take out the staircase and the whole week went flat. She tried explaining this to her brother, who said he understood completely and suggested the stair machine at his gym.

At the consultation meeting a surprising number of people spoke in favor of saving the mechanism. A teacher called it the beating heart of the district. A florist called it a witness to history. A young man who had recently opened an expensive bakery said the neighborhood was losing its authenticity. Ada knew him slightly; he had bought her old kitchen table for his window display, then sanded off the marks where her children had done their homework. The points were all entered in the minutes. At last Lecia asked Ada whether she wished to speak.

“It’s not especially old,” Ada said. “The frame is 1890. Most of the train is from 1936. I put in the escapement myself in 2008.”

People looked disappointed. The teacher lowered her phone.

“Does that mean you support the proposal?” Lecia asked.

“No,” said Ada.

“Would you like to say why?”

She had meant to talk about repairable machines, about the cost of replacing sealed units that failed. Instead she said, “There’s a stool up there that fits me.”

Somebody laughed, not unkindly. The secretary put down her pen. Ada found this surprisingly irritating. “You can take that down,” she said. The secretary did.

After the meeting a girl in a green school blazer followed Ada to the bus stop. “What happens to the old clock?” she asked. Ada explained that the faces would stay. “I know. That’s why I said the clock.” Her name was Mina. She had a gap between her front teeth and a violin case with a sticker that said FRAGILE, as if anyone opening the case might reasonably expect to find a hammer. Mina wanted the mechanism for the school. There was a landing, she explained, where they kept a dead rubber plant. The floor was probably strong enough. The plant had been very large.

Ada told her the mechanism weighed nearly half a ton. Mina considered this. The bus came and went while she considered it. Then she asked what it weighed in pieces. It was a good question. There were younger clockmakers in the city, men with excellent credentials, who would have spent ten minutes explaining why half a ton could not go up a school staircase before it occurred to them that it need not go up all at once. Ada gave Mina the shop number. “Call on Tuesday,” she said. “Have the measurements. And find out if that plant belongs to somebody.”

By Tuesday Mina had the measurements, a note from the head teacher, and the news that the plant was not dead. The school caretaker had scraped the bark with his thumbnail and found green beneath. It had been moved to a window beside the chemistry lab. Unfortunately the landing was eleven inches too narrow. “We could leave out the striking train,” Mina said. “It wouldn’t sound, but it would run.” Ada looked across the counter at this child who, four days ago, had not known that the striking train existed. “What have you been reading?” she asked. Mina unzipped the violin case. Inside lay three library books and a cheese sandwich.

It turned out there had been no violin for over a year. Mina had rented one through school, discovered she disliked it, and returned it in good condition. She kept the case because her mother, who worked nights and had a great deal to remember, sometimes still called from bed, “Don’t forget your violin.” It was easier to take the case than to go upstairs and sort out the misunderstanding. Besides, it kept the rain off her books. Ada found this arrangement both ridiculous and entirely sensible. She took Mina up the tower on Thursday, with written permission from her mother, who signed herself, Yours gratefully, though I am not clear what the violin has to do with it.

At the top Mina did not go straight to the mechanism. She went to the south face, where a little gap beside the numeral eight admitted a blade of daylight. She bent and looked through. “That’s our flat,” she said. Ada bent too. Beyond a fire escape and a treetop she saw a balcony with a blue towel over the rail. “My mum looks at the clock when she gets home. If it’s before seven she makes eggs. If it’s after seven she brings home rolls.” Mina put her hand on a girder. “I like rolls best. Can you make this side fast?”

For the next month they searched for somewhere to put the clock. The museum had no space. The library had space but no money for a structural survey. The station had space, money, and an absolute prohibition against clocks not connected to the national rail system. In the meantime the market roof began leaking over the fish stalls. The fish sellers, who had been tactfully silent during the public consultation, put buckets beside their displays and pinned photographs of the buckets to the council noticeboard. Nobody, not even the teacher who had called the clock a heart, could look at a photograph of a wet man selling wet fish under a wet umbrella without conceding something ought to be done.

The solution came from Ada’s brother. He had listened to an account of the week’s disappointments over lunch, mopping the last of his gravy with a piece of bread. “You can put it in my gym,” he said. Ada assumed he meant this in the same spirit as the stair machine. But he owned the building. The ground floor had once housed industrial laundry equipment. There were steel beams, a loading door, and a bare stretch of wall forty feet long. “People stare at that wall all day,” he said. “I’ve tried putting on the news. Nobody wants the news when they’re already doing something unpleasant.”

They went after lunch. The gym was bright and smelled faintly of oranges. Six people walked uphill on machines without advancing an inch. At the far end a very old woman was lifting a weight from the floor while a young instructor watched with the grave attention of a person observing a moon landing. Ada stood before the blank wall and imagined the clock there, its frame waist-high, all its ordinarily hidden workings visible. For the first time since the letter came she wanted, positively wanted, to take the mechanism down. Then her brother said, “Of course, it would need a face,” and the old difficulty returned in a new shape.

The original faces had to remain with the tower. A new dial could be made easily enough, but what should it look like? Her brother favored large luminous numerals, suitable for people who had removed their glasses to exercise. Mina wanted no dial, just a pair of hands traveling over the bricks. Lecia, who had secured council money for the move by filing it under both heritage retention and improvements to community health, suggested they ask the members. The members wanted a clock that went faster between six and seven in the morning. The old woman with the weights wanted a second hand. “I rest ninety seconds between sets,” she said. “I don’t care which ninety.”

One Thursday, eating lunch in her red square of light, Ada noticed that the bank wall was being painted. A platform hung across it, and two painters in paper overalls were turning the bricks pale gray. Already the color in her room had gone lavender. In another hour it would be white. She set her sandwich down and felt a foolish impulse to lean out and ask them to leave her one red square. But which square? The light came off the whole wall. To preserve exactly what she had, she would have to ask two men to stop painting, a bank to stop maintaining its property, and the sun to hold still in the sky.

She finished her sandwich. The new light was cooler but better for seeing by. On the floor beneath her stool she noticed a little brass washer that she had dropped the previous winter. It had rolled under a joist and she had sworn at it for five minutes before getting a spare from her bag. Now it shone in plain sight. She picked it up. At the shop she drilled a hole near the rim, threaded a chain through it, and hung it around her neck. It looked like nothing in particular. Her brother asked if it was some kind of medical alert.

In June they dismantled the clock. Ada labeled each part in black pencil, and Mina photographed it beside its label. The hard part was not lowering the frame. Professional riggers did that in forty minutes. The hard part was getting the stool out. It had been assembled inside the room by some ingenious predecessor and was half an inch wider than the trapdoor whichever way they turned it. Her brother suggested a saw. Ada told him where she kept it, then went down to the market and bought three peaches. When she came back the stool was on the pavement, intact. Mina had taken the trapdoor off its hinges.

They set up the mechanism at the gym behind a low glass partition. For the dial they used the wall itself, with twelve different people invited to paint one numeral each. The teacher did a neat blue two. The florist painted a five with leaves. One of the fish sellers produced an eight formed by two silver fish biting each other’s tails. Ada’s brother did the eleven, saying it was the only one he felt qualified to attempt. At six, the old woman who lifted weights painted a small black dot, perfectly round. It took her the better part of an afternoon. The dot was visible from everywhere in the room.

On the evening they started the clock, Mina came with her mother, who had changed shifts and wore a yellow dress. Lecia brought her father. He stood beside the glass for a long while, his fingers making minute adjustments to an invisible press. At seven Ada released the pendulum. The escape wheel advanced one tooth, paused, advanced again. The long hand shivered and began its almost imperceptible climb away from the six. Across town the new electric motors would already have taken the tower hands to exactly half past seven. Ada had deliberately set this clock thirty minutes slow. When somebody finally asked why, she said, “Because we started late,” and set it right.

Afterward there were paper cups of lemonade. The riggers came in from another job, still wearing their boots. The old woman did one ceremonial lift. Mina’s mother learned the truth about the violin, took a moment to count backward through an entire year of Thursday mornings, and laughed so hard that she had to sit down on Ada’s stool. Ada stood near the loading door. She had imagined this evening would feel like the end of a long repair: tools wiped, fault corrected, an orderly entry in the book. Instead there were peach stones wrapped in napkins, condensation running down the glass, and a child trying to lick the painted fish.

The following Thursday she woke early. For a few seconds she could not account for the weight in her chest. Then she remembered there was no tower to climb. She got dressed and went to the gym. Her brother had given her a key. Inside, the clock was running well. Mina had done the figures: with the weights hanging in a shallow pit where laundry water had once drained, it would need winding twice a week. Monday and Thursday would do. Ada put the handle on the square and turned it. Outside, a delivery van reversed. Upstairs, someone dropped a shoe. In the glass she saw the old woman waiting at the door, gym bag over one shoulder. Ada let her in.

“Am I early?” the woman asked.

“You’ve got a minute,” Ada said.

The woman put down her bag. Together they stood in front of the clock, waiting for the other lights to come on. It was possible, if you held quite still, to see the long hand move.

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION. A carefully shaped literary story uses a public clock and its repair to connect several characters’ routines and practical needs.

## Grounded reading
The voice is gently wry and attentive to the small facts that reveal how people live: Ada’s work boots pencilled on a wall, Mina’s violin case carrying library books, the fish sellers’ buckets beneath a leaking roof. Its pathos is understated. Ada’s attachment to the tower is less about abstract heritage than the staircase that gives shape to Thursday; the story lets that ordinary dependence matter without making it grand. The reader is invited to value care, repair, and adaptation—not as slogans, but as things people figure out together, one measurement or improvised solution at a time.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds time as something people use to organize their lives, rather than merely read from a clock: the man running late, Mina’s mother choosing eggs or rolls, the old woman timing her rests. It gives special weight to maintenance, accessible ingenuity, and objects with histories—the clock mechanism, the stool, the violin case, the brass washer. Its moral emphasis favors keeping useful things alive by changing their setting, while resisting sentimental claims about authenticity when practical needs, like the market roof, are pressing.

## Evidence line
> Take out the staircase and the whole week went flat.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the sustained pattern of understated humor, attention to ordinary objects, and practical, communal resolution makes this a distinctive sample.
